title: Data Structures & Algorithms
description: Learn DSA concepts step by step, complete topic self-checks, and unlock module assessments.

modules.title: DSA Foundations
modules.description: Build the core concepts needed to understand data structures and algorithms.

topics.title: Introduction to DSA
topics.content:
What is DSA?

Data Structures and Algorithms are the foundation of efficient problem solving in programming.

A data structure organizes data, while an algorithm defines the steps used to solve a problem.
topics.example:
Problem: Find a number in a list
Data structure: Array
Algorithm: Linear Search
keyPoints: Data structures organize data.
Algorithms solve problems.
Efficient programs depend on choosing suitable data structures and algorithms.

topics.title: Data Structures
topics.content:
Types of Data Structures

Data structures can be classified into linear and non-linear structures.

Common examples include arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees and graphs.
topics.example:
Linear: Array → Linked List → Stack → Queue
Non-linear: Tree → Graph
keyPoints: Linear structures store elements in a sequential relationship.
Non-linear structures represent hierarchical or network relationships.
The choice of structure depends on the problem.

topics.title: Linear vs Non-Linear Data Structures
topics.content:
Linear Data Structures

Elements are arranged sequentially.

Non-Linear Data Structures

Elements can have multiple relationships.
topics.example:
Linear → Array, Linked List, Stack, Queue
Non-Linear → Tree, Graph
keyPoints: Arrays and linked lists are linear structures.
Trees and graphs are non-linear structures.
Relationships are more complex in non-linear structures.

topics.title: Algorithms
topics.content:
What is an Algorithm?

An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined steps used to solve a problem.

A good algorithm should be clear, finite and effective.
topics.example:
Algorithm to find maximum:
1. Assume first element is maximum.
2. Compare with remaining elements.
3. Update maximum when required.
4. Return maximum.
keyPoints: Algorithms contain ordered steps.
Algorithms should eventually terminate.
Algorithms should produce the required result.

topics.title: Characteristics of Algorithms
topics.content:
Main Characteristics

Important characteristics include input, output, definiteness, finiteness and effectiveness.
topics.example: Input → Algorithm → Output
keyPoints: An algorithm may accept zero or more inputs.
An algorithm should produce output.
Steps should be precise.
The algorithm should terminate.

topics.title: Time Complexity
topics.content:
Time Complexity

Time complexity describes how the running time of an algorithm grows as the input size increases.

It helps compare algorithms without depending on a specific machine.
topics.example:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    cout << i;
}

Time Complexity: O(n)
keyPoints: Time complexity describes growth in execution work.
Input size is commonly represented by n.
We usually focus on the dominant growth term.

topics.title: Space Complexity
topics.content:
Space Complexity

Space complexity describes the additional memory required by an algorithm as input size increases.
topics.example:
int arr[n];

Additional space: O(n)
keyPoints: Space complexity measures memory requirements.
Auxiliary space refers to extra memory used by the algorithm.
Memory efficiency is important for large inputs.

topics.title: Big-O Notation
topics.content:
Big-O

Big-O notation describes an upper bound on the growth rate of an algorithm.

Common complexities include O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) and O(n²).
topics.example:
O(1)       → Constant
O(log n)   → Logarithmic
O(n)       → Linear
O(n log n) → Linearithmic
O(n²)      → Quadratic
keyPoints: O(1) does not depend on input size.
O(n) grows linearly.
O(n²) grows quadratically.
Big-O helps compare scalability.

topics.title: Arrays
topics.content:
Arrays

An array stores elements of the same type in contiguous memory locations in many common implementations.

Array indexing provides direct access to elements.
topics.example:
int numbers[] = {10, 20, 30, 40};

numbers[0] → 10
numbers[2] → 30
keyPoints: Arrays support indexed access.
Accessing an element by index is typically O(1).
Insertion and deletion may require shifting elements.

topics.title: Strings
topics.content:
Strings

A string is a sequence of characters.

String operations frequently appear in coding interviews and algorithmic problems.
topics.example:
string name = "CareerPilot";

name[0] → 'C'
keyPoints: Strings represent sequences of characters.
String traversal is commonly O(n).
Searching, matching and manipulation are common string problems.

modules.title: Linear Data Structures
modules.description: Learn linked lists, stacks, queues, deques and recursion.

topics.title: Linked Lists
topics.content:
Linked List

A linked list consists of nodes connected through references.

Each node commonly contains data and a link to another node.
topics.example: Head → [10|•] → [20|•] → [30|null]
keyPoints: Nodes are connected using links.
Insertion can be efficient when the position is known.
Random access is slower than arrays.

topics.title: Stack
topics.content:
Stack

A stack follows the LIFO principle: Last In, First Out.
topics.example:
Push 10
Push 20
Push 30

Pop → 30
keyPoints: Stack follows LIFO.
Push adds an element.
Pop removes the top element.

topics.title: Queue
topics.content:
Queue

A queue generally follows FIFO: First In, First Out.
topics.example:
Enqueue: 10, 20, 30
Dequeue → 10
keyPoints: Queue follows FIFO.
Insertion occurs at the rear.
Removal occurs at the front.

topics.title: Deque
topics.content:
Deque

A deque allows insertion and deletion from both ends.
topics.example: Front ← [10] [20] [30] → Rear
keyPoints: Deque means double-ended queue.
Both ends can support insertion and deletion.
It can be used to implement several queue-like behaviours.

topics.title: Recursion
topics.content:
Recursion

Recursion occurs when a function calls itself to solve smaller instances of the same problem.

A recursive solution requires a base case.
topics.example:
factorial(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
keyPoints: A recursive function calls itself.
A base case prevents infinite recursion.
The call stack stores active recursive calls.

modules.title: Searching, Sorting & Hashing
modules.description: Understand searching, sorting techniques and hash-based data structures.

topics.title: Linear Search
topics.content:
Linear Search

Linear search checks elements one by one until the target is found or the collection is exhausted.
topics.example:
[5, 8, 2, 9]
Target = 2

Check 5 → Check 8 → Check 2 ✓
keyPoints: Works on unsorted collections.
Worst-case time complexity is O(n).
Simple to implement.

topics.title: Binary Search
topics.content:
Binary Search

Binary search repeatedly divides a sorted search range into two halves.
topics.example:
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
Target = 40

Check middle → eliminate half → repeat
keyPoints: The data must satisfy the required ordering condition.
Each step eliminates approximately half the search space.
Typical time complexity is O(log n).

topics.title: Basic Sorting
topics.content:
Basic Sorting Algorithms

Bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort are common introductory sorting algorithms.
topics.example:
Before: 5 3 1
After:  1 3 5
keyPoints: Sorting arranges elements according to an order.
Basic quadratic sorting algorithms are useful for learning fundamentals.
Insertion sort can perform well on nearly sorted data.

topics.title: Merge Sort
topics.content:
Merge Sort

Merge sort uses divide and conquer: divide the array, sort the parts and merge them.
keyPoints: Merge sort uses divide and conquer.
Typical time complexity is O(n log n).
Merging combines sorted subarrays.

topics.title: Quick Sort
topics.content:
Quick Sort

Quick sort selects a pivot and partitions elements around it.
topics.example:
Pivot = 5
Smaller → 3, 2
Pivot    → 5
Larger   → 8, 9
keyPoints: Quick sort uses partitioning.
Average-case performance is commonly O(n log n).
Pivot choice influences performance.

topics.title: Hashing
topics.content:
Hashing

Hashing maps keys to positions using a hash function.

Hash tables are widely used for fast lookup operations.
topics.example:
key = 25
hash(key) → bucket index
keyPoints: Hash functions map keys to positions.
Collisions occur when keys map to the same location.
Good hashing aims for efficient lookup.

modules.title: Trees & Heaps
modules.description: Learn hierarchical data structures and priority-based structures.

topics.title: Binary Trees
topics.content:
Binary Tree

A binary tree is a tree in which each node has at most two children.
topics.example:
10
       /  \
      5   15
keyPoints: Each node has at most two children.
Children are commonly called left and right.
Trees represent hierarchical relationships.

topics.title: Tree Traversals
topics.content:
Tree Traversals

Common traversals include preorder, inorder, postorder and level-order traversal.
topics.example:
10
       /  \
      5   15

Inorder → 5 10 15
keyPoints: Preorder visits root before subtrees.
Inorder visits left subtree, root, right subtree.
Postorder visits subtrees before the root.

topics.title: Binary Search Trees
topics.content:
BST

In a binary search tree, values in the left subtree follow the ordering rule relative to the node, while values in the right subtree follow the opposite side.
topics.example:
50
       /  \
     30    70
keyPoints: BSTs maintain an ordering property.
Average operations can be efficient when the tree is balanced.
An unbalanced BST can become similar to a linked list.

topics.title: Heaps
topics.content:
Heap

A heap is a complete binary tree that satisfies a heap property.

Common forms are min-heaps and max-heaps.
topics.example:
Min Heap:
        1
       / \
      3   5
keyPoints: Min-heaps keep the smallest value at the root.
Max-heaps keep the largest value at the root.
Heaps are commonly implemented using arrays.

topics.title: Priority Queue
topics.content:
Priority Queue

A priority queue removes elements according to priority rather than simply insertion order.
topics.example:
Priority:
High → served first
Low  → served later
keyPoints: Removal depends on priority.
Heaps are commonly used to implement priority queues.
Priority queues are useful in scheduling and graph algorithms.

modules.title: Graphs
modules.description: Learn graph representations, traversal and important graph algorithms.

topics.title: Graph Basics
topics.content:
Graphs

A graph consists of vertices and edges representing relationships between entities.
topics.example:
A —— B
|    |
C —— D
keyPoints: Vertices represent entities.
Edges represent relationships.
Graphs can be directed or undirected.

topics.title: Graph Representation
topics.content:
Representing Graphs

Common representations include adjacency matrices and adjacency lists.
topics.example:
Adjacency List:
A → B, C
B → A, D
C → A
keyPoints: Adjacency lists store neighbouring vertices.
Adjacency matrices use a matrix representation.
The choice depends on graph density and operations.

topics.title: Breadth-First Search
topics.content:
BFS

Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level.

A queue is commonly used.
topics.example:
Start A
Visit A → neighbours → next level
keyPoints: BFS uses a queue.
It explores nodes level by level.
BFS can be useful for shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

topics.title: Depth-First Search
topics.content:
DFS

Depth-first search explores as far as possible before backtracking.

It can be implemented using recursion or an explicit stack.
topics.example:
Visit A
  ↓
Visit B
  ↓
Visit D
Backtrack
keyPoints: DFS goes deep before backtracking.
DFS uses recursion or a stack.
DFS is used in many connectivity and traversal problems.

topics.title: Shortest Path
topics.content:
Shortest Path

Shortest path algorithms find minimum-cost routes between vertices under specified graph conditions.
topics.example:
A --2-- B --3-- C
A ------6------ C

A to C via B = 5
keyPoints: Shortest path depends on edge properties.
Different algorithms suit different graph types.
Weights and negative edges affect algorithm selection.

topics.title: Topological Sort & MST
topics.content:
Topological Sort

Topological ordering is applicable to directed acyclic graphs.

Minimum Spanning Tree

An MST connects all vertices with minimum total edge weight in a suitable connected weighted undirected graph.
topics.example:
Tasks:
A → B → C

Possible topological order:
A, B, C
keyPoints: Topological ordering requires a directed acyclic graph.
MST connects all vertices with minimum total weight under the stated conditions.
Kruskal and Prim are common MST algorithms.

modules.title: Advanced Problem Solving
modules.description: Develop advanced problem-solving techniques used in coding interviews.

topics.title: Greedy Algorithms
topics.content:
Greedy Approach

A greedy algorithm makes a locally optimal choice at each step with the goal of obtaining a global solution.
topics.example:
Choose the currently best available option.
Repeat until the problem is solved.
keyPoints: Greedy decisions are made step by step.
A greedy strategy does not automatically work for every problem.
Correctness depends on the problem's structure.

topics.title: Dynamic Programming
topics.content:
Dynamic Programming

Dynamic programming solves problems by combining solutions to overlapping subproblems and storing results to avoid repeated work.
topics.example:
fib(5)
→ fib(4) + fib(3)
Store previously calculated results
keyPoints: DP often relies on overlapping subproblems.
Memoization stores results recursively.
Tabulation builds results iteratively.

topics.title: Backtracking
topics.content:
Backtracking

Backtracking explores possible choices and reverses a choice when it cannot lead to a valid solution.
topics.example: Choose → Explore → Reject → Undo → Try another choice
keyPoints: Backtracking systematically explores choices.
Invalid paths are abandoned.
It is common in permutations, combinations and constraint problems.

topics.title: Common Interview Patterns
topics.content:
Problem-Solving Patterns

Many coding problems can be recognized using patterns such as two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, binary search on answer and fast/slow pointers.
topics.example:
Array + contiguous range
→ Think about Sliding Window
keyPoints: Pattern recognition reduces repeated problem-solving effort.
Two pointers are useful for many array and string problems.
Sliding window is useful for many subarray and substring problems.

topics.title: Advanced Practice Strategy
topics.content:
Practice Strategy

After learning the concepts, practice problems by topic, difficulty and pattern.

Focus on understanding the approach rather than memorizing solutions.
topics.example:
Learn concept
↓
Solve easy
↓
Solve medium
↓
Review mistakes
↓
Repeat
keyPoints: Start with concept-based problems.
Review failed attempts.
Increase difficulty gradually.
Track recurring mistakes.
